{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A has a sourced, working payer model. Acquire.com publishes a $25-100/mo listing fee plus a 6-8% closing fee, and Flippa publishes $29+ listings with 5-10% success fees. Real buyers and sellers pay money in this category. Idea B states outright that no one has been shown paying for Free Pascal/Lazarus documentation.",
    "Idea A offers a revenue path that does not depend on a deal closing. A recurring or one-time listing fee, as BuyMicroStartups and Acquire.com charge, could produce a first paying customer inside 90 days even before buyer liquidity exists. Idea B's only revenue path is an unvalidated business tier.",
    "Idea A's demand evidence comes from the payer side: a seller who couldn't find buyers, and a competitor reporting 500+ daily visitors and 30 listings two weeks after launch. Idea B's demand evidence shows the docs are painful, but none of it shows anyone willing to pay. Its quotes span 2010-2024 and come from users of a free tool.",
    "Idea B's own case against points to a blocker no tooling can fix. It cites maintainer unwillingness to engage with doc fixes, and it says the Foundation funds development, not docs. It also calls the addressable developer population too small to sustain a one-person company.",
    "Idea A carries serious risks, which count against it but are not enough to lose. It faces five live competitors, three of which charge 0% or near-0% commission. Its closest comparable reports weak buyer conversion. A $750 Indie Hackers sponsorship produced 124 clicks and zero sales. Those risks still sit inside a market that pays, whereas Idea B has no evidence of a payer at all."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's payer hypothesis, a freemium model with a ~$50/month business tier, is anchored only to Read the Docs' general pricing page. The brief names no company shipping commercial Lazarus-based products that has expressed willingness to pay, so the entire revenue case rests on an assumed payer.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. Neither brief is strong for a paying customer within 90 days. Idea A wins mainly because Idea B shows no payer at all. Idea A's own evidence is discouraging: crowded zero-commission competition, the $750 test with zero sales, and buyer-side cold start. Idea A's 90-day prospects likely depend on charging sellers a listing fee rather than waiting on closing fees. The brief gives no data on listing-to-close conversion rates or sales-cycle length."
}
